extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in pop culture, media controversies, and broadcast regulation
extracted.subtask_short: encyclopedic article on Super Bowl controversy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic summary of the 2004 Super Bowl halftime show incident (Janet Jackson/Justin Timberlake), its aftermath, legal/regulatory fallout, cultural impact, and related events. The page compiles factual reporting, legal actions, industry responses, and cultural commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast indecency determination (clothing/duration/context)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC denied a complaint regarding a player's gestures because 'Moss was fully clothed at all times, and his gestures were shown for only a few seconds, thus warranting that the display was not indecent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing broadcast indecency, regulators consider factors such as whether the person was clothed, the duration the gesture/exposure was shown, and immediate context; brief, fully clothed gestures have been deemed not indecent in practice (per FCC handling of the Randy Moss incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast Decency Enforcement Act fines
rubrics_metrics.description: By June 2006, the two houses reconciled the differences in fine levels, settling for a fine of US$325,000 per violation in the Broadcast Decency Enforcement Act of 2005.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory law can set per-violation maximum fines for broadcast indecency; producers and broadcasters should be aware of these fixed per-violation penalty amounts when evaluating content risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC proposed statutory maximum fine for indecency enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC proposed the statutory maximum fine of $550,000 against Viacom-owned CBS affiliates for the apparent violation of indecency rules during the Super Bowl halftime show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory enforcement may include very large per-violation fines; note that proposed fines can change through litigation, settlement, or later legislation (the page also references subsequent settlements and court challenges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports organizations' penalties for improper language or gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: NASCAR stiffened penalties on use of improper language or gestures including larger fines, loss of points (if it occurred in a post-race interview or after the driver fell out of a race), ejection of a team from the race, or lap penalties (if in-race) under the circuit's 'detrimental to NASCAR' rule. Examples: Johnny Sauter fined US$10,000 and 25 points; Dale Earnhardt Jr. fined US$50,000 and 25 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leagues and sanctioning bodies may enforce conduct through a range of sanctions (monetary fines, points deductions, ejection, competitive penalties) under broad 'detrimental' or conduct rules; broadcasters and participants should anticipate internal sport-specific discipline beyond regulatory actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer contractual liability (breach of contract for gestures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NFL ultimately sued M.I.A. for US$1.5 million on breach of contract grounds after she 'pointed up her middle finger' during the halftime show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers may be contractually liable for actions during performances that violate terms of appearance agreements; event producers can and do seek damages for breaches tied to offensive or unauthorized conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Station/owner content control and blacklist responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The incident prompted tighter control over content by station owners and managers; Viacom ordered that Janet Jackson's singles and music videos be blacklisted from all of its properties, including CBS, MTV, and its radio station group Infinity Broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate owners and media gatekeepers may respond to controversies by restricting or blacklisting artists' content across properties; these editorial/operational decisions are an important de facto mechanism of content regulation and reputational risk management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement is subject to litigation and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC's fines and decisions in the Super Bowl case were challenged in court: appeals, remands (including consideration of FCC v. Fox Television Stations), and eventual rulings that affected fines (e.g., courts tossed or revisited fines; Supreme Court actions led to remands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory pronouncements and proposed penalties can be altered, vacated, or remanded through judicial processes; compliance planning should account for the potential for enforcement actions to change through litigation and precedent.
